subject: film
title: German Expressionism (c. 1919–1931): painted sets, chiaroscuro shadows, and the anxious screen of Weimar
dek: After World War I defeat and amid hyperinflation, Weimar studios built distorted worlds on painted canvas and lit them with stark contrasts. Robert Wiene's The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920), F.W. Murnau's Nosferatu (1922), and Fritz Lang's Metropolis (1927) turned psychological horror and social anxiety into visual style. By the early 1930s sound arrived, the Nazis rose, and many filmmakers fled.

thumb.alt: Black-and-white portrait of Fritz Lang in the 1920s, looking to the side with a serious expression.

hero.alt: Weimar-era street scene in Berlin showing the Café Kranzler on Kurfürstendamm with pedestrians, early automobiles, and urban bustle.
hero.caption: Café Kranzler on Kurfürstendamm, Berlin, during the Weimar Republic years. This is a historical street photograph from the German Federal Archive, not a film still. The same Berlin streets and café culture that appear in this documentary image were the social world that German Expressionist filmmakers inhabited and sometimes placed on screen.
hero.credit: Unknown photographer / German Federal Archive / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 3.0 DE

honesty: “German Expressionism” is a historians' and critics' label borrowed from painting and theater, not a self-proclaimed school with membership cards. The cluster usually begins around The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) and runs through the late silent and early sound era into roughly 1931 (M, Fritz Lang's first sound film, often marks the late edge). Not every Weimar film was Expressionist — plenty of comedies, melodramas, and street films worked other styles — and the painted-set distortion of Caligari was not repeated in every titled film. F.W. Murnau preferred location shooting and moving cameras; Lang's Metropolis is studio spectacle more than painted canvas. Useful dates: Caligari 1920, Nosferatu 1922, The Last Laugh 1924, Metropolis 1927, M 1931. Studios: Decla-Bioscop (which merged into UFA), UFA itself as the major Weimar conglomerate. Many filmmakers fled after 1933 when the Nazis consolidated control. Film stills from these silents are often still managed commercially even when underlying negatives are public domain in some jurisdictions; this lesson prefers public-domain portraits and set stills already on Wikimedia Commons, plus the Berlin street photograph above, each captioned as what it actually shows. No AI people.

timeline.label: Defeat, revolution, Weimar begins
timeline.detail: Germany loses World War I, the Kaiser abdicates, revolution and counterrevolution convulse Berlin. The Weimar Republic begins amid political chaos, territorial losses, and reparations burdens. Studios that had produced wartime propaganda pivot to civilian stories and experimental forms.

timeline.label: Decla-Bioscop / Caligari
timeline.detail: Erich Pommer's Decla-Bioscop produces The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (Robert Wiene, 1920) with a script by Carl Mayer and Hans Janowitz. Painted sets by Hermann Warm, Walter Röhrig, and Walter Reimann turn a fairground murder story into crooked streets and jagged roofs. The film becomes an international postcard of Weimar anxiety.

timeline.label: UFA consolidates / Nosferatu
timeline.detail: Universum Film AG (UFA) absorbs Decla-Bioscop and grows into the dominant German studio. F.W. Murnau's Nosferatu (1922), an unlicensed Dracula adaptation shot partly on location, uses Expressionist lighting and shadow rather than fully painted sets. Max Schreck's vampire becomes an icon.

timeline.label: Hyperinflation / The Last Laugh
timeline.detail: Hyperinflation peaks in 1923; a wheelbarrow of marks buys a loaf of bread. Studios struggle with costs and foreign competition. Murnau's The Last Laugh (1924), scripted by Carl Mayer, tracks a hotel doorman's fall with an “unchained camera” (Karl Freund cinematography) and almost no intertitles — Expressionist psychology through camera movement.

timeline.label: Stabilization / Metropolis / late silents
timeline.detail: Currency stabilizes; UFA invests in spectacle. Fritz Lang's Metropolis (1927), co-written with Thea von Harbou, builds a futuristic city of towers and underground machines — Expressionist scale and chiaroscuro applied to science fiction. Murnau makes Faust (1926) and departs for Hollywood. Paul Leni emigrates. The style begins to fragment.

timeline.label: Sound arrives / M / political collapse
timeline.detail: The Depression hits; political violence intensifies. Sound cinema complicates silent visual rhetoric. Lang's M (1931), with Peter Lorre as a child murderer, uses sound and shadow in a Berlin underworld — late Expressionist style meeting early sound. The Weimar Republic is collapsing; the Nazis will seize power in 1933.

timeline.label: Emigration / Hollywood exile
timeline.detail: Hitler becomes Chancellor; Joseph Goebbels controls film through the Reich Film Chamber. Lang, Billy Wilder, Robert Siodmak, Edgar G. Ulmer, and many others flee to France, Britain, and Hollywood. Expressionist lighting and urban anxiety seed film noir abroad; in Germany the style is buried under propaganda.

fun_fact.title: Caligari's painted sets were partly a budget solution
fun_fact.text: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari's wildly distorted streets and buildings — painted shadows, crooked windows, impossible perspectives — are often read as pure Expressionist intent. They were also cheap. Post-war German studios faced material shortages and tight budgets; painting shadows and angles directly onto canvas flats cost less than building elaborate three-dimensional sets and lighting them conventionally. Necessity and aesthetics collaborated. The result looked so strange that it became the movement's visual signature, even though later Expressionist films often returned to more realistic sets and relied on lighting for mood. The set still here shows those famous painted shadows and angles; the style was born from defeat, inflation, and invention working together.

image.alt: A scene from The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari showing the distorted painted set of Holstenwall with crooked buildings, sharp angles, and shadows painted onto the walls.
image.caption: Public-domain still from Robert Wiene's The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (Decla-Bioscop, 1920) showing the painted fairground town of Holstenwall. The jagged roofs, painted shadows, and impossible geometry were partly aesthetic choice and partly economic necessity in postwar Germany. Not a modern photograph — a frame from the 1920 film.
image.credit: Robert Wiene / Decla-Bioscop / Wikimedia Commons / public domain (film published 1920)

glossary.explain: Historians' label for a tendency in Weimar-era German cinema (roughly 1919–1931) using distorted visuals, stark lighting, and psychological themes — borrowed from Expressionist painting and theatre.
German state from 1919 (post-WWI) to 1933 (Nazi seizure of power). Political instability, hyperinflation, cultural flowering, and eventual collapse frame the era's cinema.
Robert Wiene's 1920 film about a hypnotist, a somnambulist, and fairground murders, shot with painted distorted sets in Expressionist style. Often treated as the movement's founding text.
F.W. Murnau's 1922 unauthorized adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula, shot partly on location with Expressionist lighting. Max Schreck plays Count Orlok.
Fritz Lang's 1927 UFA spectacle about a futuristic city divided between workers below and elites above. Co-written with Thea von Harbou; monumental Expressionist design and early science fiction.
Fritz Lang's 1931 early sound film about a child murderer (Peter Lorre) hunted by police and criminals in Berlin. Late Expressionist shadow and urban anxiety meeting synchronized sound.
F.W. Murnau's 1924 film about a hotel doorman's social fall, shot mostly without intertitles using Karl Freund's mobile "unchained camera". Expressionist psychology through movement and framing.
Director (1873–1938) of The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari. Continued working in Weimar cinema but never repeated Caligari's visual extremity or fame.

Director (1888–1931) of Nosferatu, The Last Laugh, Faust, and later Hollywood films (Sunrise). Preferred location shooting and moving cameras over painted sets; Expressionist mood through light and camera.
Director (1890–1976) of Metropolis, M, Die Nibelungen, and many others. Co-wrote with Thea von Harbou. Emigrated after 1933; made film noir and genre films in Hollywood.
Screenwriter (1894–1944) of Caligari, The Last Laugh, Sunrise (for Murnau in Hollywood), and other key films. Master of visual storytelling; often minimized intertitles.
Screenwriter and novelist (1888–1954), Fritz Lang's collaborator and wife (until 1933). Co-wrote Metropolis, M, Die Nibelungen. Later joined the Nazi Party; Lang emigrated, von Harbou stayed.
Cinematographer (1890–1969) of The Last Laugh, Variety, Metropolis, and many others. Pioneered mobile camera techniques; emigrated to Hollywood, shot Dracula (1931) and later worked in television.
Producer (1889–1966) at Decla-Bioscop and UFA. Produced Caligari, Metropolis, and many others. Championed international co-productions and spectacle; fled in 1933.
Actor (1893–1943) who played Cesare the somnambulist in Caligari and many other Weimar roles. Emigrated; later played Major Strasser in Casablanca.
Actor (1879–1936) who played Count Orlok in Nosferatu. The bald vampire look became an Expressionist horror icon.
Actor (1904–1964) who played the child murderer in M. Emigrated after the Nazis rose; later a Hollywood character actor (The Maltese Falcon, Casablanca).
Universum Film AG — the dominant German studio conglomerate of the Weimar era, absorbing Decla-Bioscop and producing Metropolis and many others. Nationalized under the Nazis.
German production company that made Caligari and other early Weimar films; merged into UFA in 1921.
Italian term for strong contrasts between light and dark. German Expressionist films used extreme chiaroscuro lighting to create mood, shadows, and psychological depth.
Caligari's signature technique: painting shadows, angles, and distortions directly onto flat canvas scenery instead of building realistic three-dimensional architecture.
Marketing term for Karl Freund's mobile camera work in The Last Laugh, freed from static tripod positions to follow characters and create subjective points of view.
Economic collapse in early Weimar Germany, peaking in 1923 when currency became worthless. Shaped studio economics and national anxiety that fed Expressionist themes.

American and French 1940s–50s crime cinema characterized by cynicism, night photography, and urban shadows. Often traced to Weimar Expressionist emigres (Lang, Siodmak, Ulmer) bringing their lighting and mood to Hollywood.
Roughly contemporaneous 1920s Soviet film movement emphasizing editing; related capsule on this site. Eisenstein and others studied German techniques; different political contexts.
Late-1950s/early-1960s French filmmakers (Truffaut, Godard) who studied and wrote about classic German cinema; related capsule on this site.

sections.title: Defeat, revolution, and a broken industry

blocks.text: German cinema before 1918 was already an industry. Studios in Berlin, actors, serials, melodramas, and wartime propaganda were facts of commercial production. The Kaiserschlacht broke that continuity. Germany lost World War I in November 1918, the Kaiser abdicated, revolution convulsed the streets, and the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 imposed reparations, territorial losses, and a clause declaring German war guilt. The Weimar Republic began amid political chaos: Spartacist uprising and Freikorps violence in January 1919, the Kapp Putsch in 1920, assassinations of politicians, competing visions of what Germany should become. Studios that had made patriotic features pivoted to civilian stories, but the economic ground was unstable. Hyperinflation would peak in 1923 when a wheelbarrow of marks bought a loaf of bread.

Material shortages shaped production. Film stock, electricity, and set-building resources were scarce and expensive. That scarcity is part of why The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari's painted sets looked so strange: painting shadows and angles directly onto canvas flats cost less than constructing elaborate three-dimensional architecture and lighting it conventionally. Aesthetics and economics collaborated. The Treaty had also restricted German film exports, so studios initially aimed at a domestic audience nursing defeat and processing trauma. When Caligari premiered in February 1920, critics saw crooked fairground streets, a hypnotist, a somnambulist murderer, and an asylum frame story that some read as allegory for authority, madness, and obedience. Historians later borrowed the label "Expressionism" from painting and theater to name what they were watching on screen.

The "before" is therefore double: a commercial studio habit built before the war, and the defeat-and-revolution rupture that left filmmakers working with tight budgets, unstable politics, and a public that had just survived trenches, occupation, hunger, and civil street fighting. Expressionism did not invent German cinema. It was one response — distorted, psychologically heightened, visually radical — to that breakage.

sections.title: From Caligari's painted shadows to Metropolis towers and M's sound

blocks.text: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari is the usual hinge. Produced by Erich Pommer's Decla-Bioscop, scripted by Carl Mayer and Hans Janowitz, directed by Robert Wiene, and designed by Hermann Warm, Walter Röhrig, and Walter Reimann, the film told a fairground horror story inside sets where perspective was impossible, shadows were painted onto walls, and streets tilted at nightmare angles. Conrad Veidt played Cesare, the somnambulist kept in a cabinet by Werner Krauss's Dr. Caligari and sent out to murder. The frame story added by Pommer revealed the main tale as the delusion of an asylum inmate, defusing some of the script's original critique of authoritarian control. That frame remains controversial among critics. The painted Holstenwall fairground, however, became the movement's postcard: jagged roofs, crooked doors, Expressionism as visual synonym for Weimar anxiety.

blocks.alt: Distorted painted set from The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari with sharp angles, painted shadows, and impossible architecture.
blocks.caption: Public-domain still from Robert Wiene's The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (Decla-Bioscop, 1920): the painted town of Holstenwall. The crooked buildings, flat perspective, and painted shadows are the film's signature style — Expressionist aesthetic and postwar budget necessity working together.
blocks.credit: Robert Wiene / Decla-Bioscop / Wikimedia Commons / public domain (film published 1920)

blocks.text: Not every Expressionist film repeated Caligari's painted extremity. F.W. Murnau preferred location shooting and camera movement. Nosferatu (1922), an unlicensed Dracula adaptation, took Max Schreck's bald vampire Count Orlok into real landscapes and lit interiors with stark chiaroscuro rather than painting every shadow. The film was eventually destroyed in a copyright lawsuit brought by Bram Stoker's estate, but prints survived abroad. Murnau's The Last Laugh (1924), scripted by Carl Mayer and shot by Karl Freund with a mobile "unchained camera", followed a hotel doorman's social fall through subjective camera work and almost no intertitles — Expressionist psychology rendered through framing, movement, and lighting instead of sets. Faust (1926) returned Murnau to spectacle with elaborate effects before he left for Hollywood, where he made Sunrise (1927) with Mayer, blending Weimar visual poetry and American resources.

blocks.alt: Black-and-white portrait of F.W. Murnau in a suit, 1928.
blocks.caption: F.W. Murnau in a 1928 publicity photograph from his Hollywood years. By this date Nosferatu and The Last Laugh were behind him; he was shooting American films with Expressionist sensibility. Not a film still — a studio portrait of the director.
blocks.credit: Unknown photographer / Wikimedia Commons / public domain (U.S. publication, no copyright renewal)

blocks.text: Fritz Lang built monumental scale. Die Nibelungen (1924) adapted medieval German legend with stylized compositions and vast sets. Metropolis (1927), co-written with Thea von Harbou and produced by UFA at enormous cost, imagined a futuristic city split between towers and underground machine halls, workers and elites, with Brigitte Helm playing both the saintly mediator Maria and the false robotic Maria. The Tower of Babel prologue and the Moloch machine sequence are Expressionist spectacle — chiaroscuro shadows and distorted perspectives applied to science fiction on an industrial budget. The film nearly bankrupted UFA; audiences were mixed. Later critics treat it as late silent excess and prescient dystopia. By 1931 sound had arrived. Lang's M, with Peter Lorre as a child murderer hunted by police and Berlin's criminal underworld, used Expressionist lighting and urban dread in a talkie — whistling, footsteps, crowd noise, and a kangaroo court in an abandoned factory. The Weimar Republic was collapsing; Hitler would become Chancellor in 1933. M is often treated as the movement's late edge, where sound met the old visual grammar and political catastrophe loomed.

blocks.alt: Still from Metropolis showing a monumental tower set with crowds of workers at the base during the Tower of Babel sequence.
blocks.caption: Public-domain still from Fritz Lang's Metropolis (UFA, 1927) showing the Tower of Babel construction sequence. Monumental Expressionist design, vast crowds, and dystopian future city — late silent spectacle on UFA's biggest budget. This frame comes from the restored legendary lost footage; the film's production nearly bankrupted the studio.
blocks.credit: Fritz Lang / UFA / Wikimedia Commons / public domain (film published 1927)

sections.title: Wiene, Murnau, Lang — and a wider crew of writers, designers, actors

blocks.text: Deepen Wiene, Murnau, and Lang first. Robert Wiene directed Caligari but never repeated its visual extremity; his later work is competent Weimar melodrama without the painted nightmare. F.W. Murnau moved from Nosferatu's location horror to The Last Laugh's subjective camera work, then to Faust's elaborate spectacle and finally to Hollywood, where Sunrise won early Academy Awards before his death in a 1931 car accident. Fritz Lang co-wrote with Thea von Harbou on Die Nibelungen, Metropolis, and M; after the Nazis rose, Lang claimed Goebbels offered him control of the German film industry despite his Jewish heritage. Lang emigrated, first to France then to Hollywood, where he made film noir and genre films through the 1950s. Von Harbou stayed in Germany, joined the Nazi Party, and continued working; the marriage ended in 1933 with Lang's departure.

blocks.alt: Black-and-white portrait of Fritz Lang in the 1920s, looking to the side with a serious expression.
blocks.caption: Fritz Lang in a 1920s portrait. Director of Metropolis, M, Die Nibelungen, and later Hollywood film noir. This photograph predates his emigration; not a still from his films.
blocks.credit: Unknown photographer / Wikimedia Commons / public domain (published before 1928)

blocks.text: Name the writers and designers: Carl Mayer scripted Caligari, The Last Laugh, and Sunrise — a master of visual storytelling who often minimized intertitles. Hans Janowitz co-wrote Caligari's original script and opposed the asylum frame. Hermann Warm, Walter Röhrig, and Walter Reimann painted Caligari's sets. Karl Freund shot The Last Laugh, Variety, and parts of Metropolis with mobile camera innovations, then emigrated to Hollywood where he shot Dracula (1931) and later worked in television. Erich Pommer produced Caligari, Metropolis, and many others as UFA's key figure; he championed international ambition and fled in 1933.

Name the actors who became icons: Conrad Veidt played Cesare and later emigrated, appearing in The Man Who Laughs (Hollywood, 1928) and Casablanca (1942) as Major Strasser. Werner Krauss played Dr. Caligari and stayed in Germany, acting in Nazi propaganda. Max Schreck's bald, rat-like Count Orlok in Nosferatu became the vampire image that rivaled Bela Lugosi's later Dracula. Peter Lorre's Hans Beckert in M — whistling, sweating, cornered — introduced the actor to international audiences before he fled and became a Hollywood character face. Brigitte Helm's dual role as Maria and the robot in Metropolis made her a star; she retired before World War II. Emil Jannings of The Last Laugh won Hollywood's first Best Actor Oscar, then returned to Germany and worked under the Nazis.

blocks.alt: Max Schreck as Count Orlok in Nosferatu, bald with pointed ears and clawed hands, staring forward.
blocks.caption: Public-domain still from F.W. Murnau's Nosferatu (Prana Film, 1922): Max Schreck as Count Orlok. The vampire's bald head, elongated fingers, and rodent-like features became an Expressionist horror icon. The film was an unlicensed Dracula adaptation; Stoker's estate sued and ordered prints destroyed, but copies survived abroad.
blocks.credit: F.W. Murnau / Prana Film / Wikimedia Commons / public domain (film published 1922)

blocks.text: Look sideways without turning the decade into a worksheet. In the Soviet Union, roughly contemporaneous with Caligari and Metropolis, Lev Kuleshov's workshop was demonstrating the Kuleshov effect and Sergei Eisenstein was building Battleship Potemkin (1925) and October (1928) from collision montage — a related capsule on this site. Soviet theorists studied German films as technique and as ideological opponents: they admired Griffith's crosscutting and German camera craft while rejecting what they saw as bourgeois psychology and decorative distortion. The two movements are neighbors and rivals, not parent and child. Both responded to postwar rupture (defeat in Germany, revolution in Russia) with radical form, but German Expressionism leaned toward nightmare and individual psyche while Soviet montage aimed at collective argument and material dialectics.

In France the 1920s saw Impressionist cinema — Germaine Dulac, Jean Epstein, Abel Gance — experimenting with subjective camera work, optical effects, and rhythm. Gance's Napoleon (1927) used rapid cutting and widescreen triptychs; Epstein's The Fall of the House of Usher (1928) borrowed Gothic atmosphere but with different visual language than German shadows. In Hollywood the studio system refined continuity editing and star power; German emigres would arrive after 1933 and seed film noir's shadows and cynicism (Robert Siodmak's The Killers, Edgar G. Ulmer's Detour, and Lang's own Hollywood work). In Japan the 1920s were peak silent years with benshi narrators and studio genres developing parallel to European experiments. In Britain documentaries and Ealing features worked social observation; in Mexico the Golden Age was beginning. Same calendar, different industrial roofs and political pressures.

What traveled from Weimar was influence, not a franchise. Universal Horror in 1930s Hollywood — Dracula (1931, shot by Karl Freund), Frankenstein, The Mummy — borrowed Expressionist lighting and emigre talent. Film noir inherited chiaroscuro, urban dread, and fatalism from the filmmakers who fled. French New Wave critics later wrote about Lang and Murnau as auteurs and moral witnesses; a related capsule on this site. The style's afterlife in classrooms, festivals, and genre DNA is a migration story as much as an aesthetic one.

sections.title: Emigration, noir shadows, and long genre afterlives

blocks.text: By 1933 the Weimar Republic was over. Hitler became Chancellor; Joseph Goebbels took control of German cinema through the Reich Film Chamber. Jewish filmmakers and those politically suspect were expelled or chose exile. Fritz Lang, Billy Wilder, Robert Siodmak, Edgar G. Ulmer, Paul Leni (who had already died in 1929 in Hollywood), Peter Lorre, Conrad Veidt, Karl Freund, and many others fled to France, Britain, and Hollywood. Those who stayed worked under propaganda demands or made entertainment that avoided politics. Leni Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will (1935) showed what monumental cinema looked like under the Nazis — spectacle serving the state, Expressionism's distorted psychology replaced by regimented masses and Führer worship.

The emigres seeded American film noir: shadowy cinematography, urban paranoia, morally ambiguous protagonists, and stories of entrapment. Siodmak's The Killers (1946), Ulmer's Detour (1945), Lang's The Big Heat (1953), Wilder's Double Indemnity (1944) — Weimar lighting and fatalism meeting American crime stories. Horror continued the line: Universal's Dracula and later creature features, Roger Corman's Poe adaptations, and Tim Burton's Expressionist-influenced design for Edward Scissorhands and The Nightmare Before Christmas. French New Wave critics wrote about Metropolis and M in Cahiers du Cinéma before making their own films; later cinephile directors from Martin Scorsese to Guillermo del Toro cited the Weimar silents as foundational. Film schools still teach Caligari's painted sets, Nosferatu's vampire iconography, and Metropolis's dystopian city as basic visual literacy.

The label remains useful if you keep it fuzzy — a stylistic and thematic cluster responding to Weimar Germany's defeat, instability, and trauma, roughly 1919 to 1931, closed by sound technology and political catastrophe, then scattered by emigration into global influence. Not a single manifesto, not every German film, but a visible enough tendency that critics and historians still argue about its edges and its politics.

If a fairground town's streets are painted crooked and its shadows are drawn onto canvas instead of cast by lights, what anxiety or truth about authority, obedience, and reality is the film asking you to see that a realistic set would hide?
